prompt: What question does XP ask that Scrum and Kanban leave alone?
hint: They organise work; XP looks somewhere else.

choices.text: How long an iteration lasts
choices.why: Every method has an answer; it is not XP's distinctive question.

choices.text: How many cards fit in a column of the board
choices.why: That is Kanban's limit.

choices.text: What the code needs for late change to be cheap
choices.why: Right. XP is about the technical practices that make the manifesto's promise affordable.

choices.text: Who orders the backlog
choices.why: Scrum answers that with the Product Owner.

prompt: Match each feedback loop to how fast it answers.
hint: From the inside of the stack out.

prompt: Which value was added in the second edition of Extreme Programming Explained?

choices.text: Predictability
choices.why: Not one of XP's values at all.

choices.text: Feedback
choices.why: Feedback was a value from the first edition.

choices.text: Respect
choices.why: Right. Communication, simplicity, feedback and courage were already there.

choices.text: Courage
choices.why: Courage was in the first edition.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the inner three loops are what flatten the cost-of-change curve?
hint: What does a team know within minutes of a change?

choices.text: Late changes are checked in minutes
choices.why: Right. Knowing quickly what broke is what makes changing working code cheap.

choices.text: They remove the need for an iteration
choices.why: XP keeps iterations; the inner loops do not replace them.

choices.text: They make estimates more precise
choices.why: Estimates are not what the loops change.

choices.text: They let the customer skip the review
choices.why: The customer still sees software each iteration.

prompt: Put one turn of the test-first loop in order.
items: Write a test and watch it fail
Write the least code that passes
Improve the code with the tests passing
trap: The code comes after the failing test, never before it.

prompt: In the lesson's first run, why did the test fail?
hint: Read the last line of the traceback.

choices.text: Python 3.13 cannot run unittest
choices.why: It ran the test and reported the error.

choices.text: The test had a typo in its name
choices.why: The name was fine; the import failed.

choices.text: The PERT formula returned the wrong number
choices.why: There was no formula yet to return anything.

choices.text: The module it imports did not exist yet
choices.why: Right. ModuleNotFoundError: no module named 'estimate' — the code had not been written.

prompt: What does pert(3, 5, 13) return?
What did writing the second test first force, according to the lesson?
hint: pert(13, 5, 3) would have returned a number.

choices.text: A decision about nonsense input
choices.why: Right. The function now refuses figures in the wrong order instead of returning a plausible number.

choices.text: Removing the first test, which had become redundant
choices.why: Both tests stay and both pass.

choices.text: A second module, separate from estimate.py
choices.why: The fix went into the same function.

choices.text: A faster version of the formula that runs in constant time
choices.why: Speed was never in question.

prompt: A team's tests break every time somebody restructures code without changing what it does. What does the lesson say is wrong?
hint: Tests can make change more expensive.

choices.text: There are too few tests
choices.why: More tests of the same kind would break more often.

choices.text: They test the mechanism instead of the behaviour
choices.why: Right. Such tests punish refactoring, the opposite of their purpose.

choices.text: The team writes the tests first
choices.why: Writing them first is not what ties them to the structure.

choices.text: Refactoring should be banned
choices.why: Refactoring is the third step of every turn.

prompt: What did Williams and colleagues find in their 2000 study of pairs?
hint: A trade, not a free lunch.

choices.text: Half the effort, because two people type faster
choices.why: Pairs spent more effort, not less.

choices.text: Somewhat more effort, fewer defects
choices.why: Right. Roughly 15% more person-hours, with code that had fewer defects.

choices.text: No measurable difference of any kind
choices.why: They measured both effort and defects.

choices.text: Twice the effort and no difference in quality
choices.why: The effort was far less than double, and quality improved.

prompt: Which benefit of pairing does the lesson call the easiest to see in a team?

choices.text: Cheaper hardware, since pairs share a computer
choices.why: A trivial saving next to two salaries.

choices.text: At least two people know every part
choices.why: Right. That is collective code ownership, and it takes the sting out of somebody leaving.

choices.text: Faster typing
choices.why: Typing was never the bottleneck.

choices.text: Fewer meetings
choices.why: Pairing changes how code is written, not the meeting load.

prompt: For which work does the lesson say mob programming is most used?

choices.text: Overnight production support
choices.why: Waking the whole team is not what mob programming is for.

choices.text: Typing up meeting minutes
choices.why: Not programming at all.

choices.text: Routine changes that everybody already knows how to make
choices.why: That is where pairing, let alone mobbing, pays least.

choices.text: Hard decisions, unfamiliar code, onboarding
choices.why: Right. Few teams mob all day; many mob when a decision needs everybody.

prompt: A team has a CI server that builds every branch, and its branches live three weeks. Is it doing continuous integration?

choices.text: Only if it also pairs
choices.why: Pairing is a separate practice.

choices.text: Yes, if the builds are under ten minutes
choices.why: Fast builds of long branches are still late integration.

choices.text: No: it merges every three weeks
choices.why: Right. Continuous integration means merging at least daily; the server is a tool.

choices.text: Yes: it has a CI server
choices.why: A tool's name does not make the practice.

prompt: The main line has been red since lunch. What does the practice say comes first?

choices.text: Open a ticket for the next Sprint
choices.why: A day of red blocks everybody now.

choices.text: Fix or revert the change that broke it
choices.why: Right. A main line that stays red stops being one.

choices.text: Carry on merging and fix it at the end of the day
choices.why: Every merge on top of a red build hides the next failure.

choices.text: Disable the failing test
choices.why: That hides the breakage instead of fixing it.

prompt: A feature takes two weeks to build. How does the lesson keep integration continuous anyway?

choices.text: Release it half-done and fix it in production
choices.why: Users would see half a feature.

choices.text: Split the team so nobody else touches that code
choices.why: Isolation postpones the conflict; it does not remove it.

choices.text: Keep it on a branch until it is finished
choices.why: That is the late integration the practice exists to avoid.

choices.text: Merge it unfinished behind a flag that keeps it off
choices.why: Right. Merging and releasing become two separate decisions.

prompt: How many minutes does XP's second edition name for a build to be fast enough?
Match each of the three Cs of a story to what it is.

pairs.right: A reminder in a sentence or two
The tests that say it is done

prompt: In XP's planning game, who decides how long a story will take?
hint: Each side has knowledge the other lacks.

choices.text: The manager, by averaging both sides' figures
choices.why: The game has no averaging; each side keeps its own decision.

choices.text: The customer, who is paying for it
choices.why: Paying for it does not give knowledge of the cost.

choices.text: Whoever wrote the story card
choices.why: Writing the card gives no authority over the estimate.

choices.text: The developers
choices.why: Right. The customer decides value and order; the developers estimate cost.

prompt: A team meets every date by working weekends for a month. What does XP's sustainable-pace rule say this hides?

choices.text: A wrong plan
choices.why: Right. The date is met and the estimate that caused it is never revised.

choices.text: Nothing; the dates were met
choices.why: Meeting the date by overtime is how the problem stays hidden.

choices.text: A team that is not committed enough to the product
choices.why: Overtime shows commitment; what it hides is the plan.

choices.text: Too many pairs working on the same story
choices.why: Pairing has nothing to do with the hours worked.

prompt: What precondition of small releases does the lesson say is easy to miss?
hint: Think of a weekend of manual steps.

choices.text: The team has to work in Sprints of one week
choices.why: XP's iterations are not what makes releases cheap.

choices.text: The customer has to sign every release
choices.why: Signing is not the precondition the lesson names.

choices.text: Releasing has to be cheap
choices.why: Right. A release that costs a weekend will not be done often.

choices.text: Every story has to use the Connextra template
choices.why: The template is unrelated to releasing.

prompt: Put Beck's four rules of simple design in priority order.
trap: Fewest elements comes last: it never justifies removing something the first three need.

prompt: A team applies YAGNI to how clinics' data is separated, and builds for one clinic. Why does the lesson say this is where an architect is right to push back?

choices.text: Architects should make every decision up front
choices.why: Only the irreversible ones get early thought.

choices.text: The tests would not pass
choices.why: Tests can pass for one clinic and still leave the trap.

choices.text: YAGNI is wrong in general and should be dropped
choices.why: It is right for decisions that are cheap to change.

choices.text: The decision is expensive to reverse later
choices.why: Right. YAGNI is an argument about cheap decisions; separating tenants is not one.

prompt: Improving the structure of code without changing what it does, in small steps with the tests passing, is called ___.
Which practices form XP's three inner feedback loops? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The release
choices.why: The outermost loop, months.

choices.text: The iteration
choices.why: An outer loop that every method has.

choices.text: Test-first programming
choices.why: Yes: minutes.

choices.text: Pair programming
choices.why: Yes: seconds.

choices.text: Continuous integration
choices.why: Yes: hours.

prompt: A manager wants to cut pairing, tests and refactoring to deliver more features this quarter. What does the lesson predict?

choices.text: Fewer defects, since there is less code to test
choices.why: Less testing means more defects reach users.

choices.text: A faster build, since the tests are gone
choices.why: A faster build that checks nothing is not a gain.

choices.text: The cost of a late change creeps back up
choices.why: Right. The curve those practices flattened rises again, slowly.

choices.text: More features with no consequence
choices.why: The consequence is real and delayed.
